claims.text: Rapid quenching from the melt followed by controlled isothermal annealing can direct phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
This heat-treatment sequence directs phase evolution by modifying diffusion kinetics and nucleation rates.
The initial as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy has a mixed or metastable disordered microstructure.
Rapid quenching freezes the high-temperature phase distribution.
Intermediate-temperature isothermal annealing promotes selective nucleation and growth of desired phases.
Rapid quenching minimizes equilibrium phase formation.
Suitable annealing temperatures and times enable diffusion-mediated transformation without detrimental coarsening or unwanted phase formation.
Nucleation sites and evolving phase interfaces mediate transformation toward a controlled multiphase structure.
Rapid quenching suppresses early equilibrium transformations and locks in a high-energy state.
Subsequent annealing promotes selective nucleation and diffusion-driven phase growth.
The proposed treatment will produce a more uniform and tailored multiphase microstructure than the as-cast baseline.
The proposed treatment will enhance strength and toughness relative to the as-cast state.
The proposed treatment will reduce the amount or detrimental effects of brittle phases.
A quench that is too slow may permit equilibrium-like phase evolution.
Misoptimized annealing temperature or duration may produce unwanted coarse phases.
Optimal quench rates, annealing parameters, and stabilized phases for this alloy system remain uncertain and require experimental calibration.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as already as-cast, while the intervention begins by quenching directly from the melt. Applying that intervention to an already as-cast specimen would require an unstated remelting step, and the structural-mediator field instead describes transformation directly from the as-cast microstructure.
